segments.narration: Scotland buried its finest rock art on purpose in 1965. A slab at Faifley, forty-two feet across, carved with about ninety cups and rings.
Bronze Age hands cut those spirals into the rock. Reverend James Harvey recorded the stone in 1887, and curious visitors never stopped arriving.
Then came the graffiti, scratched right beside the prehistoric carvings. Why would anyone protect a masterpiece by hiding it under earth completely?
One archaeologist had already made things worse. In 1937 Ludovic Mann painted bright lines across the carvings to test an eclipse-prediction theory.
Mann's own measurements disproved him. Glasgow archaeologists re-exposed the slab in 2016, scanned every groove in 3D, then deliberately covered it over again.

verdicts.claim: The Cochno Stone at Faifley measures about 42 by 26 feet and carries roughly 90 carved cup-and-ring marks; it was deliberately reburied in 1965.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives 42 by 26 feet (12.8 by 7.9 m), about 90 carved indentations, and reburial in 1965; the Glasgow and Live Science reports confirm the 1965 burial was deliberate, on Euan MacKie's recommendation.

verdicts.claim: The carvings are Bronze Age, and the Rev. James Harvey documented the stone in 1887.

verdicts.note: The 2016 re-excavation reports describe 19th- and 20th-century graffiti etched alongside the prehistoric swirls.

verdicts.claim: In 1937 Ludovic Maclellan Mann painted lines across the carvings to test a link to astronomical phenomena.
verdicts.note: Both the Glasgow release and Live Science report Mann's 1937 painted measuring lines and his eclipse-prediction idea, which Brophy says Mann's own data disproved.

verdicts.claim: University of Glasgow archaeologists re-exposed the stone in 2016, recorded it digitally in 3D, and then reburied it.
verdicts.note: The University of Glasgow release describes the two-week 2016 excavation with Factum Foundation 3D scanning and the subsequent reburial for protection.
